content: To improve clinical care and monitoring, as well as enhance the use of data, healthcare professionals should provide supportive advice and recommendations. Pharmacists and pharmacy technicians or assistants play a critical role in dispensing medications, managing drug-related toxicities, reporting adverse drug reactions, offering adherence counseling, monitoring, and recording antiretroviral (ARV) dispensing in pharmacy records. Facility-based lay providers are responsible for enrolling patients, completing demographic information on patient cards, transferring this information to registers, providing adherence counseling, educating patients on treatment literacy, assessing adherence through methods like pill counts, and tracking patients lost to follow-up (LTFU). To strengthen human resource development, training programs should be designed using patient monitoring data to identify areas of weakness and strong performance. Training should be integrated into pre-service education, in-service training, and ongoing professional development. Trainees should be supported, and staff trained in medical, nursing, or pharmacy programs should take refresher courses or continuing education. Opportunities outside formal training, such as case reviews, experience sharing, clinical mentoring, educational presentations, conferences, and cross-site visits, should also be utilized. Clinical mentoring and supportive supervision are essential for building the capacity, motivation, and confidence of less experienced clinical providers. A clinical mentor, who is an experienced clinician, provides ongoing training, advice, and support to help providers develop skills, grow professionally, and deliver better care. Mentors meet regularly with providers to review clinical cases, answer questions, solve problems, provide feedback, and assist with case management. They may be formally assigned or volunteer based on personal interest and can include district hospital clinical providers who mentor through visits and long-distance exchanges. These visits should include observing case management, reinforcing staff skills, reviewing HIV patient cards and ART registers or electronic equivalents, conducting clinical case reviews, holding clinical team meetings, and documenting each visit with recommendations. Many countries with a high burden of HIV are transitioning from paper-based systems to electronic medical records (EMRs) to address challenges such as difficulty retrieving data, the time and effort required to maintain paper systems, the need for integration across service areas, and increasing investments in digital health innovations. While EMRs are being rolled out to support HIV patient monitoring and management, coverage across facilities remains suboptimal in many settings. Consequently, some countries may still rely on aggregate data systems for reporting HIV program performance. Guidance on transitioning to EMRs, including issues related to unique identifiers (UIDs), data system interoperability, and data security and confidentiality, is provided in Chapter 6. Establishing high-quality individual-level data is critical for improving national and global reporting. Accurate patient-level data from HIV monitoring systems, entered into HIV patient cards or directly into EMRs, is essential. Clinical teams should prepare for visits by selecting cases for review, such as those recently initiated on ART, routine or challenging cases, or deaths. In some cases, inviting clients back to the clinic during a mentor's visit can facilitate consultation and avoid referrals. Recommendations from mentoring should be integrated into quality management and improvement activities at health centers. The transition to digital health systems is driven by the need for accurate and efficient data retrieval, integration across services, and the adoption of digital innovations. However, many countries still face challenges in achieving optimal coverage of electronic systems. Improved data linkage between HIV and related infections, such as tuberculosis (TB), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), hepatitis B and C, and cervical cancer, can enhance program impact and efficiency. Surveillance systems should monitor these infections as part of HIV prevention and treatment programs, given their shared modes of transmission and overlapping risk profiles. Women living with HIV are at a significantly higher risk of cervical cancer, with 85% of cases occurring in sub-Saharan Africa. WHO guidelines recommend integrating cervical cancer screening and treatment into routine HIV care. Similarly, testing and treatment for hepatitis B and C should be included in HIV programs, particularly for key populations such as people who inject drugs, sex workers, men who have sex with men, and individuals in prisons or other closed settings. STI surveillance is a critical component of HIV epidemic control and program management. Prompt diagnosis and treatment of STIs can reduce HIV transmission and improve health outcomes. WHO recommends periodic testing for asymptomatic STIs in high-risk populations, including men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, sex workers, and pregnant women. Integrating STI, hepatitis, and cervical cancer data into HIV surveillance systems can help identify gaps in service access, coverage, and quality, ultimately improving resource allocation and decision-making. Globally, an estimated 5% of cervical cancer cases are attributable to HIV, and women living with HIV have a six-fold higher risk of cervical cancer. Integrated health services and better data systems are essential for achieving universal health coverage and addressing the substantial burden of related infections among people living with HIV.
